walkthroughs.body_html: BedZED (Beddington Zero Energy Development) opened in 2002 in Sutton, London. It features super-insulated homes, passive solar design, wind cowls for ventilation, on-site renewable energy, water recycling and car clubs. Residents have around 60 percent lower carbon footprints than the UK average and a strong community culture.

Curitiba, Brazil, pioneered Bus Rapid Transit in the 1970s. Dedicated bus lanes, tube-stations and integrated tickets give metro-style speed at a fraction of the cost. Around 70 percent of commuters use the system. Combined with extensive parks and waste-for-food exchange schemes it is a benchmark for sustainable urbanism.

Dense roads, buildings and dark roofs absorb sunlight, while reduced vegetation cuts evapotranspiration cooling. Vehicle exhaust and air conditioning add waste heat. Cities can be 1 to 5 C warmer than the countryside, harming health during heatwaves. Green roofs, urban trees, reflective surfaces and water features all help cool cities.

mcqs.q: Why are tropical rainforest soils often nutrient-poor despite abundant vegetation?
options: Rainforests are deserts most of the year.
One is for plants, the other for animals.
Rapid decomposition and uptake mean nutrients cycle quickly through living biomass, not soil.
Rainforests have rich soils because they are productive.

mcqs.q: Why is ice-albedo feedback a positive feedback loop?
options: Because warming is positive (a good thing).
Less ice means less reflective surface, so more sunlight is absorbed, causing more warming and more melting.
Because polar bears help spread heat.
One is for plants, the other for animals.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between in-situ and ex-situ conservation?
options: Because polar bears help spread heat.
In-situ protects species in their natural habitat; ex-situ removes them to controlled settings like zoos or seed banks.
One is for plants, the other for animals.
They are alternative names for the same approach.
